text: Windows Firewall doesn't apply one fixed rule set to a machine — it switches between three profiles automatically depending on how trusted the current network is, and inbound traffic is treated very differently from outbound traffic by design, not by accident. This lesson covers those three profiles, that inbound/outbound asymmetry, and what Microsoft Defender Antivirus's real-time and cloud-delivered protection actually watch for on top of all of it.

Domain is the most permissive profile, active when the machine can reach its domain controller. Private covers networks a user has manually marked as trusted, like a home network. Public, the most restrictive, covers untrusted networks like airport Wi-Fi. Inbound traffic is blocked by default unless a rule explicitly allows it; outbound traffic is allowed by default unless a rule explicitly blocks it — because something reaching in uninvited is far more dangerous than software already running reaching out.

A laptop with file sharing enabled for the Domain and Private profiles stops answering those same requests the instant it connects to airport Wi-Fi, because Windows automatically switches to the Public profile and that inbound rule is disabled there by default. Nothing was changed manually — the firewall just applied a different, more restrictive rule set for a network it has no reason to trust.

Microsoft Defender Antivirus's real-time protection continuously scans files the moment they're opened, run, downloaded, or modified — no manual scan required. Cloud-delivered protection goes further: when Defender can't confidently classify a file locally, it checks it against Microsoft's cloud threat intelligence, often blocking brand-new malware within hours of it first appearing, well before a traditional signature update would ever catch it.

Firewall profiles and Defender protect the machine while it's running and connected to a network. Neither one protects the data sitting on its disk if the machine itself is lost or stolen outright.
